typical_aromatherapy_uses: Skin-focused aromatherapy and topical formulas; commonly promoted for acne, athlete's foot, minor skin concerns and antimicrobial personal care.
evidence_summary: NCCIH: small amount of evidence suggests topical tea tree oil may help acne and athlete's foot, but more studies are needed. IMARC lists tea tree as the largest essential-oil product segment in 2025.
safety_notes: Do not swallow. Oral intake can cause serious toxicity. May cause skin redness or irritation, especially if oxidized/old. Use extra caution around small children and pets.
suggested_use_notes: Use externally only; dilute for most skin use and patch test first. Avoid diffuser use in households where sensitive children, pets or respiratory-sensitive people may be exposed.
confidence: High for market rank; Medium for topical acne/athlete's-foot evidence

typical_aromatherapy_uses: Relaxation routines, sleep support, stress relief, massage blends and bath products.
evidence_summary: NCCIH: aromatherapy benefits for anxiety, stress, pain and sleep remain unclear, though some people report improved quality of life; oral lavender products have limited evidence for anxiety. IMARC lists lavender as the second-largest product segment in 2025.
safety_notes: Aromatherapy is considered possibly safe but may cause headache or coughing. Topical products can trigger allergic skin reactions. Possible interaction concern with sedatives; limited pregnancy/breastfeeding safety data.
suggested_use_notes: Diffuse lightly or use diluted in carrier oil. Avoid treating anxiety, insomnia or depression solely with lavender without professional care.
confidence: High for market rank; Low-to-Medium for aromatherapy clinical evidence

typical_aromatherapy_uses: Mood-lifting scent, room diffusion, home fragrance, cleaning blends and massage blends.
evidence_summary: Cleveland Clinic lists orange oil as commonly used to reduce anxiety and pain and to kill bacteria; Fact.MR identifies citrus oils as a major essential-oil product category.
safety_notes: Cold-pressed citrus oils may increase sun sensitivity depending on composition. Skin irritation is possible. Avoid ingestion unless supervised by a qualified professional.
suggested_use_notes: Use in short diffusion sessions or diluted topical blends; avoid sun/UV exposure after topical citrus oil use unless the product is verified non-phototoxic.

typical_aromatherapy_uses: Mental refreshment, fatigue support, headache massage blends, nausea support and digestive-wellness products.
evidence_summary: NCCIH: enteric-coated peppermint oil may improve IBS symptoms in adults; limited evidence suggests inhaled peppermint may reduce chemotherapy-related nausea/vomiting; topical use may help tension headaches.
safety_notes: Can cause heartburn, nausea, abdominal pain, dry mouth or allergic reactions when taken orally. Skin rashes/irritation possible. Do not apply to face of infants or young children due to menthol breathing risk.
suggested_use_notes: For aromatherapy, inhale gently and avoid use around very young children. For topical use, dilute well and keep away from eyes and mucous membranes.
confidence: High for IBS oral capsule evidence; Medium for nausea/headache aromatherapy/topical uses

typical_aromatherapy_uses: Seasonal respiratory comfort, steam-style inhalation, muscle rubs and spa blends.
evidence_summary: Cleveland Clinic describes eucalyptus as commonly used for stuffy-nose comfort, pain relief and antimicrobial/anti-inflammatory purposes; Fact.MR lists eucalyptus among major product categories.
safety_notes: Do not ingest. Can have dangerous effects in children and pets. Must be diluted before topical use; may irritate skin or airways.
suggested_use_notes: Use low amounts in diffusion or steam-like inhalation; avoid around infants, young children, pets, asthma-sensitive people or seizure-prone individuals unless cleared by a clinician.

typical_aromatherapy_uses: Mood support, nausea support, cleaning blends, room diffusion and freshness blends.
evidence_summary: NCCIH lists lemon among oils used in aromatherapy; Cleveland Clinic lists lemon oil as commonly used for anxiety/depression, pain, nausea and antibacterial purposes, and cites limited aromatherapy research involving cognitive function.
safety_notes: Can increase photosensitivity and sunburn risk after topical use. Skin irritation possible. Avoid ingestion without professional guidance.
suggested_use_notes: Diffuse in small amounts or use diluted in topical blends; avoid direct sun/UV exposure after topical application.

typical_aromatherapy_uses: Stress support, mood blends, relaxation rituals and perfumery-style aromatherapy.
evidence_summary: NCCIH lists bergamot among oils used in aromatherapy; Cleveland Clinic lists bergamot oil as commonly used to reduce anxiety, lift mood and lower blood pressure.
safety_notes: Many bergamot oils are phototoxic unless bergapten-free/FCF. May irritate skin. People using blood-pressure medication should be cautious about unsupported therapeutic use.
suggested_use_notes: Prefer diffuser use or properly diluted topical use with bergapten-free oil; avoid sun/UV exposure after topical application unless non-phototoxic status is confirmed.

typical_aromatherapy_uses: Meditation, grounding blends, skin-care aromatherapy, sleep and mood routines.
evidence_summary: Cleveland Clinic lists frankincense as commonly used for inflammation, mood and sleep, with additional preliminary areas such as asthma and gum health.
safety_notes: May irritate skin if not diluted. Evidence for disease treatment is limited; do not replace asthma, inflammatory or dental treatment.
suggested_use_notes: Use in diffuser or diluted topical blends. Treat claims as wellness-supportive, not curative.

typical_aromatherapy_uses: Focus, alertness, hair/scalp blends, muscle/joint massage and mood support.
evidence_summary: Cleveland Clinic lists rosemary oil as commonly used for brain function, hair growth, pain/stress reduction, mood and joint inflammation.
safety_notes: Avoid during pregnancy or if you have epilepsy or high blood pressure unless advised by a clinician. Skin irritation possible; dilute before topical use.
suggested_use_notes: Use lightly for diffusion or in diluted topical blends. Avoid high-dose or prolonged exposure for sensitive users.

botanical_name: Cedrus atlantica / Juniperus virginiana and related species
typical_aromatherapy_uses: Sleep blends, calming routines, grounding blends, deodorant/insect-repellent style formulas and scalp products.
evidence_summary: NCCIH lists cedarwood among oils used in aromatherapy; Cleveland Clinic lists cedarwood as commonly used for sleep and anxiety and notes antioxidant/antibacterial properties.
safety_notes: Can irritate skin; do not ingest. Species and chemistry vary, so safety and scent profile differ by product.
suggested_use_notes: Use diluted on skin or diffuse in low amounts, especially at bedtime. Confirm botanical species for formulation work.
